channel.title: CrosseRoads Guides
channel.description: Practical guides on career discovery and college admissions, from Dr. Kisa Crosse.

item.title: College for Undocumented and Mixed-Status Families
item.description: Federal aid is closed, but in-state tuition, state aid and private scholarships are open in many places. What is possible, and where to get proper legal advice.

item.title: Senior Year Stress: What Is Normal and What Is Not
item.description: Application season is genuinely hard, and some distress is expected. A family physician on where the line sits, and what to do when a student crosses it.

item.title: The 30-Day Career Exploration Challenge
item.description: Your career does not have to be decided today. Your goal is to identify pathways worth exploring — and one focused month is enough to start.

item.title: Junior Year: The Head Start That Makes Senior Year Easy
item.description: The work completed during junior year lays the groundwork for a successful senior year — service, leadership, testing strategy, and a balanced college list.
The three lanes of college money — federal aid, institutional aid, and outside scholarships — and the follow-up habits that keep offers from slipping away.

item.title: The Early Action Advantage: Why Applying Early Can Mean More Offers — and More Money
item.description: Early Action applications often bring earlier decisions, better scholarship consideration, and a far less stressful senior year. Here is how families use them well.

item.title: How to Choose a Career That Fits Who You Are: The 7-Factor Method
item.description: Most people pick careers based on one factor — salary, or a subject they liked. A better fit comes from looking at seven factors together.

item.title: College for Students Who Have Been in Foster Care
item.description: Automatic independent status on the FAFSA, dedicated federal grants, and state tuition waivers exist — and are missed constantly, because nobody tells the student they qualify.

item.title: The Empty Nest Nobody Prepared You For
item.description: Everyone plans the move-in day. Almost nobody plans the drive home, or the six weeks after it. A physician and mother on what actually helps.

item.title: What Mental Health Support Actually Exists on Campus
item.description: Counselling centres, disability accommodations, and the paperwork that decides whether a college may talk to you at all. What to sort out before move-in day.

item.title: Parent Burnout Is Not a Character Flaw
item.description: The adult in this process carries the money, the deadlines and the emotional weather, usually while working. What burnout looks like, and what actually helps.

item.title: Helping Without Taking Over
item.description: The line between supporting a student and running their application is thinner than it looks, and crossing it costs them more than the help was worth.

item.title: First-Generation Students: The Things Nobody Tells You
item.description: The academic work is rarely what trips up a first-generation student. It is the unwritten rules — office hours, aid renewal, what a dean is for — that nobody thought to explain.

item.title: The FAFSA When Parents Are Separated or Divorced
item.description: The parent who reports on the FAFSA is not necessarily the one with custody, or the one who claims the student on taxes. Getting this wrong delays aid for months.

item.title: Sleep Is Not the Thing You Do After the Work
item.description: Teenagers need eight to ten hours and almost none get them. A physician on why sleep is the highest-leverage change available in senior year.

item.title: How Much Student Debt Is Too Much?
item.description: A borrowing total is an abstraction. A monthly payment against a starting salary is a decision. Here is how to turn one into the other before anyone signs.

item.title: What a First Job Teaches That No Class Does
item.description: Part-time work in high school is not a distraction from the application. Handled well, it is one of the most revealing things on it.

item.title: The Transfer Route: Two Years Local, Same Degree, Far Less Debt
item.description: Starting at community college and transferring can produce the identical bachelor’s degree for a fraction of the cost — if you confirm which credits transfer before you register.

item.title: The Scholarships Almost Nobody Applies For
item.description: National scholarships draw tens of thousands of applicants. The $500 award from a local community foundation sometimes draws four. Here is where to look.

item.title: How to Ask a Teacher for a Recommendation Letter
item.description: A teacher with the right information writes a specific letter. A teacher without it writes a polite one. The difference is a single sheet of paper and four weeks of notice.

item.title: What Labour Market Data Actually Tells a Family
item.description: Median pay, projected growth and typical entry education are published free for every occupation in America. Most families never look, and decide on anecdote instead.

item.title: Demonstrated Interest: Does It Actually Matter?
item.description: Some colleges track whether you opened their emails. Others ignore it entirely. How to find out which is which, without wasting your senior year performing enthusiasm.

item.title: When Your Student Has No Idea What They Want
item.description: "I don’t know" is not avoidance and it is not a crisis. It usually means a student has never been shown enough of the world to have an opinion about it.

item.title: How to Appeal a Financial Aid Offer (and Why Most Families Never Try)
item.description: Financial aid is calculated from a tax year that may no longer describe your life. A short, factual letter asking for a professional judgement review is free, and it works more often than families expect.

item.title: The Fifteen-Minute Conversation That Changes a Career Plan
item.description: Asking an adult about their job is the cheapest, fastest career research there is — and teenagers almost never do it. Here is the message to send and what to ask.

item.title: What a Campus Visit Should Actually Tell You
item.description: The official tour is a sales pitch walking backwards. Here is how to spend two hours on a campus and come away knowing something the brochure could not tell you.

item.title: Who Does What: Dividing the College Process
item.description: Most family arguments about applications are really disputes about ownership that nobody wrote down. Fifteen minutes with a pen settles almost all of them.

item.title: How to Read a Financial Aid Award Letter
item.description: Award letters are written to look generous. Line up four of them in the same format and one number tells you what each college actually costs your family.

item.title: Good Careers That Do Not Need a Four-Year Degree
item.description: Skilled trades, allied health, apprenticeships and certificate programmes lead to solid, well-paid work — often faster and with far less debt. Where to look, and what to check.

item.title: How to Build a College List That Is Actually Balanced
item.description: A list of eight reaches is not a list, it is a lottery ticket. How to sort schools into likely, target and reach — and why affordability belongs in that sorting.

item.title: Getting Through Senior Year as a Single Parent
item.description: One adult, one calendar, and a process designed for households with two of everything. What can be delegated, what cannot, and where to find help that costs nothing.

item.title: Sticker Price Is Nobody’s Real Number
item.description: The published cost of a college is a starting figure most families never pay. Here is how to find what you would actually be charged — before you rule a school in or out.

item.title: Choosing a Major Without Choosing a Life
item.description: Most people do not work in the field they majored in, and most majors do not lock anyone into anything. What a seventeen-year-old actually needs to decide, and what can wait.

item.title: Junior Year Is the Year That Decides Your Options
item.description: Senior year is mostly paperwork. Junior year is where the transcript, the test scores and the college list are actually built. Here is what to do, month by month.

item.title: Telling Your Teenager What You Can Actually Afford
item.description: Most families avoid the number until April, then deliver it as a disappointment. Saying it in junior year turns it into a planning constraint instead.
